title: Your Organic Label Is a Lie | Food Industry Exposed
summary: Podcast arguing the organic label has been corrupted by big agriculture and lobbying, and that buying direct from local farms is the only trustworthy option.

assertions.quote: big corporations that pay lobbyists to to change the rules to allow certain things to sneak by
concoct an organic um cocktail that you could still put on food that grows faster but it's actually worse than usual pesticide
I can make a lot of money if I just label that thing certified organic
if they're using organic to signal synthetic fertilizers that are just as bad for us as the other ones

verdicts.note: The USDA organic rules prohibit synthetic fertilizers apart from a few listed exceptions such as some micronutrients.
Organic standards prohibit all mineral N fertilisers plus KCl and superphosphate, prescribing manure, compost and legumes instead (background statement of the standards).
The review notes mineral nitrogen fertilisers are not permitted under organic farming standards (illustrated by Finland's selenium-fortified N fertiliser being unavailable to organic farms).

7 CFR 205.203(e)(1) bars any fertilizer containing a synthetic substance not on the National List; only listed synthetics such as micronutrients for documented deficiencies and pH-adjusted fish products are allowed (205.601(j)), so general synthetic fertilizers such as synthetic nitrogen are not permitted.
The National Organic Program text quoted by ERS says synthetic fertilizers may not be used in organic production.

assertions.quote: And it's been cleared for putting being put on organic food.

verdicts.note: At least one plant-lipid shelf-life coating has an organic-approved formulation, and coatings from allowed substances can be used on organic produce.

assertions.quote: the best place to get anything you're eating is directly from the producer from the person who grew it
you probably aren't even getting what you think you're getting because we have no, you know, country of origin labeling laws

verdicts.note: Generic grass-fed claims describe diet and are approved company by company; only some third-party certifiers also require pasture.
